Bonnie Irwin   Private practice in Vermont. She received her master’s degree in psychoanalysis from the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis (BGSP), where she is currently a candidate in the doctor of psychoanalysis program. She has published on the use of psychoanalytic training in a classroom setting.

An extensive case report on the modern psychoanalytic treatment of a psychotic patient. The author presents the history of the patient’s emotional life as it emerged through the transference-countertransference dynamic, which developed (“matured”) during this long treatment. Telling this patient’s treatment history in this way, almost as a detailed memoir of the rise and development of the analyst’s own countertransference states, proves to be a particularly illuminating way of making the patient’s essential self present and alive in the reader’s awareness. This account is supported by extensive reference to clinical writings on narcissism and the narcissistic defenses.

What can a theory and practice developed by a Jewish physician in early 20th-century Vienna for the cure of modern neurotics, and meditation techniques developed by the Brahman caste in 6th century BC India, possibly have in common? T.K.V. Desikachar and Hellfried Krusche seem to sense commonalties between them; Freud and Yoga is their attempt to discover and describe that common ground. The book takes the examination of the ancient sage Patanjali’s Yoga Sutras as its jumping-off point for exploring how the two philosophies compare. Freud and Yoga is structured as a dialogue between Krusche, a European psychoanalyst, and Desikachar, a yoga master. Their musings on the two subjects should be enlightening for both yoga practitioners and psychoanalysts. The ancient text consists of close to 200 sutras (which are terse aphorisms that together constitute a methodical elucidation of what yoga is, how it is realized, and the obstacles to its realization). In the Mind Fields: Exploring the New Science of Neuropsychoanalysis. Casey Schwartz. New York: Pantheon, 2015. 219 pp.

George Ernsberger

George Ernsberger

George Ernsberger  

Casey Schwartz is a popular journalist who has academic credentials in both neuroscience and psychoanalysis. This is an introduction for lay readers to a burgeoning body of work being done at the borders of these adjoining bodies of thought—work we might think of at this stage as a sort of land-clearing. Schwartz commands a clear, free-flowing style that can be a wonderful medium for untangling intricate concepts and writings (for example: she presents almost in passing a concise summing-up of Freud's “Project for a Scientific Psychology” that strikes me as startlingly accurate, clear, and fair). She leads us into this terrain hesitantly at first, reporting her own second thoughts and backtracking as she proceeds. It's a narrative strategy one's come to identify as bloggish—and to tire of pretty quickly—but it soon repays the reader's patience handsomely; you may be surprised at how well prepared you are to follow the interpenetration of these systems of thought when she begins to present it.

She reads voraciously, but then she also finds a couple of interesting people to ask questions of and pay extended attention to as they search for an intellectual territory where these two ongoing endeavors could proceed together, complementing as well as complicating each other. The first, the South African psychoanalyst Mark Solms, is also a neurosurgeon.

Nahaleh Moshtagh   Clinical psychologist in private psychotherapy practice in Tehran. She is a graduate of Iran University of Medical Sciences and an analytic candidate at the Academy of Applied and Clinical Psychoanalysis (ACAP). Dr. Moshtagh is the executive director of HamAva Insitute in Tehran. She has published on mother-child relations and is the translator into Farsi of books including Adam Phillips’s Winnicott.

Despite the disagreeable cliché that psychoanalysis is a mother bashing theory, the mother has been a latecomer to the field. Till the end, the Freudian theory did remain father centered and paternal. Freud, who knew the castrating mother very well, didn’t give the mother a central place in his theory, and didn’t feel this absence was worthy of elaboration. It was Abraham who introduced the concept of the “bad mother” when he was working with Freud, and later as Klein’s analyst influenced her return to the mother as the most important object in the child’s encounter with the world. Yet, Klein’s notion of mother remained as a phantasy object in the child’s internal world of object relationships. Even Winnicott who seems to be concerned with the external mother in the environment, is concerned primarily with the pre-oedipal mother in relation to the infant. The Oedipal mother of the later years who may actively become the subject of seduction, rivalry, and envy in her relationship with her daughter or son is only seen in case reports, but rarely in psychoanalytic theorizing. It seems safer to talk about the absence of a good mother rather than about the presence of a bad mother. Bad mother is a concept that should be inferred rather than presented. Sources of Suffering. Salman Akhtar. London: Karnac Books, 2014, 192 pp.

Mary Landers

Mary Landers

Mary Landers  

Akhtar, whose target reader is the novice in the field of psychoanalysis, starts from the premise that suffering is necessary for psychic development. The book is an attempt to codify into the grammar of psychoanalysis six sources of suffering: fear, greed, guilt, deception, betrayal, and revenge. The purpose and function of each of these emotions are explored in some breadth and depth, but he immediately establishes that his discussion will focus and will elaborate on the pathological suffering that we come in contact with in the treatment room. The list is neatly divided in half, distinguishing those sources of suffering that beset the sufferer from within—“suffering tolerated” (fear, greed, guilt)—from those aiming outward—“suffering inflicted” (deception, betrayal, revenge).

He refers to Freud in every chapter and also provides examples of current studies in brain science with regard to fear and related mind states. Each section garners the ideas of notable psychoanalytic thinkers to help render good comparative conclusions. This style is natural to Akhtar, who is the author of Comprehensive Dictionary of Psychoanalysis. Attempts at a comprehensive discussion of the particular emotions discussed in this book are made. Akhtar is most engaging when he sticks with the psychoanalytic, and less so when he becomes sociologically and politically polemical.

Jon Dzitko  

In “Freud and the Scene of Writing” Jacques Derrida expressed his understanding of Freud’s idea of psychical genesis as, “delay which is in the beginning” (1978, p. 203). What is this delay? It signifies the later effects of emergence—a process, a trace, a Being not defined by presence—found in the psychic processes that (re)create the sexual subject—Freud’s Nachtraglichkeit. The concept is taken up by Jean Laplanche in his “general theory of seduction” and is translated as afterwardness (1999, p. 260). Laplanche’s general theory of seduction and his theory of the “enigmatic signifier/messages” are at the heart of Quindeau’s thesis regarding subjectivity and sexuality (i.e. the sexual). At every significant juncture in this book, one is brought back to Quindeau’s (re)articulation of Laplanche’s theory of being overcome by the touch, fantasy, desires of the Other (der Andere, the other person), and the cumulative effects that form the capacity to “delay” and continually reinscribe, throughout life, the all-too-powerful early enigmatic messages of sexuality. Subjectivity is held hostage to the “alien-ness” (1997, p. 654) of the Other (das Andere, the unconscious). The psyche becomes a (re)writing machine which is not just seduced once, but constantly re-worked—a type of inter-desiring text—since new pleasures and experiences can be (re)inscribed through these acts of seduction and unconscious (re)inscriptions, “we may still maintain that the first time of the contact between two forces, repetition has begun” (1978, p. 202).

Quindeau explores the held historical assumptions and theoretical conceptualizations of sexuality and development found constituting the psychoanalytic subject. Quindeau, like Lacan, problematizes the assumptions of the relational and object schools’ grand narratives of a subject’s psychic journey toward individualization and independence. In place of this Western presupposition of self-sufficiency—an autological subjectivity—she offers a hybrid of Lacanism that emphasizes dependency on the Other (not the Saussurian langue, but more aligned with Julia Kristeva’s (1984) semiotic of touch, caress, rhythmization, and the early eroticization of the body)

Eugene Goldwater MD

Eugene Goldwater

1581 Beacon Street
Brookline, MA 02446

Eugene Goldwater   Psychiatrist and psychoanalyst who practices in Hadley and Brookline, MA and teaches at the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis. He has taught, lectured and written about numerous subjects, including fantasy, impulsivity and addiction, childhood and maturation, marriage and parenting, violence, and happiness.

In a presentation to psychoanalytic educators and students, the author presented the reflections from which he has adapted this article. In it, he carefully elaborates both developmental theory and practice guidance from his personal life experiences and clinical observations. He shows that desire—active longing for the fulfillment of a wish—is always accompanied by conflict, because wishes always offer both reward and risk. When the conflict is unconscious the real risks are greater and the rewards less certain. Bringing a conflict to conscious awareness may improve the chances of getting what one really wants, but at the initial cost of emotional effort and pain, particularly in mastering the essential ability to say “no.”

Psychoanalysis in an age of accelerating cultural change: Spiritual globalization. Neil Altman. New York: Routledge, 2015. 152 pp.

William Sharp

William Sharp

William Sharp  

Altman's Psychoanalysis in an Age of Accelerating Cultural Change (2015) is a continuation of his twenty-five years of thinking about the application of psychoanalytic principles on several planes. He addresses these principles as he understands them with respect to social and cultural phenomena outside and apart from the treatment process as well as their clinical application within it; he also considers the significance of cultural influences on the personalities of the patients we strive to understand and to devise treatment responses for. The thesis of his book supports psychoanalysis as a method of inquiry and way of understanding. Altman advocates moving psychoanalytic principles out of the consulting room and into our communities, schools, and corporations. He applies his psychoanalytic lens to the world we all observe. By challenging our ideas Altman means to show that psychoanalytic theory is not only applicable, but indispensable both to working with and on our patients and understanding our wider world of cultural change.

Applying psychoanalytic ideas outside of the treatment room inevitably leads to the difficult task of defining psychoanalysis. As his definition in this book, Altman uses Freud's study of transference and resistance (1914/1962), and the science of unconscious mental processes (1923/1962).

Uta Gosmann  

The Letter

He was waiting for a reply; a reply that failed to come. Why?

He waited and it tore him up. Every day filled with hope and then crushed with disappointment.

What should he do? Wait, wait, there was no other solution. The days passed … the letter arrived but it was already too late, he could no longer remember what letter it was, he read it … thought about how much he had suffered, and he ripped it up, stunned by his own stupidity.

Synthesis

The severed hands, gripping the steering wheel, had such longing for him that they dripped blood until they reconstituted his image.

The Involution of the Species

It neither assimilated nor evacuated, it was only capable of processes of incorporation and excretion: nothing that heralded the semblance of a thought.

These short and dense narratives are examples of reverie, dreamt by Antonino Ferro while listening to patients.* Reverie is a core concept in Bionian and post-Bionian psychoanalysis and important in Ferro's and Civitarese's latest book, The Analytic Field and Its Transformations (2015). Reverie describes both a mental production evoked by the analytic process and a key form of analytic intervention. Reveries are miniature narratives, sometimes as compressed as an aphorism, organized around a central metaphor that expresses, one could say, feeling-thoughts or thought-feelings. In “The Letter,” the speaker spends much time waiting for a letter that, by the time he receives it, has become irrelevant. The letter, as central metaphor, is the object of misdirected desire and turns out not to be what the speaker wanted. The narrative evokes feelings of folly, futility, and wastefulness.

*Ferro, A. (2015). Reveries: An unfettered mind. Trans. Neil Davenport. London: Karnac. 4, 39, 46.100

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

In Memoriam: June Bernstein and Murray H. Sherman

Modern Psychoanalysis, Volume 40.2, Dedicated to June Bernstein

June Bernstein, who died in the night of December 21-22, 2016, was instrumental in the birth and growth of this journal and became its editor in 2005. As valuable as was her mastery of both Freudian and modern psychoanalytic theory and history, Dr. Bernstein’s essential gift as an editor might have been the energy and enthusiasm that fueled her encouragement and development of younger writers. She was, of course, a prolific writer for the journal herself, publishing many seminal theoretical and clinical articles that were collected as a monograph as our Volume 38, Number 1, dated 2013. In her writing and in conversation Dr. Bernstein also consistently called upon her great memory and love for specific works of Freud throughout her lifetime.

Dr. Bernstein was a dedicated teacher, supervisor, and research adviser at both the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies and the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis, where she was honored as Professor Emerita. She was an excellent teacher, erudite, quite irreverent, opinionated and very funny. Her many contributions to both schools, and to the field of psychoanalysis at large—and especially, for this moment, to this journal—live on, providing energy and direction to us all.

Robert Marshall

Robert Marshall   Faculty member, training analyst, and supervisor at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies. He is a diplomate in clinical psychology of the American Board of Professional Psychology and was chair of the publications committee, Division 39 of the American Psychological Association. He is the author of more than 30 professional chapters and articles. His books include Resistant Interactions: Child, Family, and Psychotherapist and The Transference-Countertransference Matrix: The Cognitive-Emotional Dialogue in Psychotherapy, Psychoanalysis, and Supervision. He is in private practice in New York City.

The influence of Hungarian psychoanalysts on Hyman Spotnitz is studied from three points of view: The personal and professional effect of his analyst, Lillian Delger Powers, and his supervisors, Sandor Rado and Sandor Lorand, all of whom had close associations with both Sigmund Freud and Sandor Ferenczi; the theoretical and clinical effect of others such as Margaret Mahler, Franz Alexander, and Melanie Klein, who had been influenced by Ferenczi; and a comparison of Spotnitz and Ferenczi in terms of their personal and professional orientations.

The author presents clinical material from a case that spans over twenty years. A therapeutic relationship begins when the patient is an adolescent boy. Repeated terminations are the hallmark of the case, which communicate to the analyst the patient's conflict around leaving, being left, and his ultimate psychic separation from his family of origin, and the painful but necessary journey from adolescence into independent adulthood. Techniques of modern psychoanalysis are demonstrated in treating the patient through emotional communications rather than cognitive discourse.

From Primitive Fears to the Safety of Metaphor**

Josie Oppenheim MA NCPsyA LP

Josie Oppenheim

415 West 23 Street
New York, NY 10011
Phone: 212 206 6578
Email: analyst@josieoppenheim.com

Josie Oppenheim   Training analyst on the faculty of the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies (CMPS) and was cofounder and artistic director of the Stella Adler Conservatory Theater. She has published numerous articles on psychoanalytic and cultural topics, lectures widely, and is a recipient of the Phyllis W. Meadow Award for excellence in psychoanalytic writing. She is in private practice in New York City.

Psychoanalytic reconstructions of primitive mental states describe the infant's fears of “falling forever” and dread of an “endless void,” along with fantasies of omnipotent control. The author suggests that such primitive anxieties represent the result of an evolutionary loss that was visited upon our species as we hovered between nonhuman primate and human being. It is, the author observes, an essential feature of our species that we must turn away from the concrete in favor of a metaphoric engagement with self and other and she proposes a theory of why this is so. Condensing evolutionary time, she creates a myth-like narrative to show how metaphoric thinking might reasonably have become, through the processes of natural selection and adaptation, critical to the survival of our species.

The author provides a theoretical and practical overview of modern psychoanalysis as a school of thought, and its place among current psychoanalytic theories. Back in the day (I am talking about 30+ years, here) analytic training at CMPS began with a two year “field placement” in the “back ward” of a psychiatric institution. Although those back wards, for the most part, no longer exist, the basic modern psychoanalytic tenet that observing psychosis is a singularly illuminating way to understand all forms of human behavior holds true today as much as ever.

A naive and newly minted social worker fresh out of graduate school, I was eager, if trepidatious, about beginning my placement at The Manhattan State Psychiatric Center, on Wards Island; a bus ride and a world away.

Field placement students there were assigned patients to follow in the following manner: We were told to “mingle” in the day room and see which patients might gravitate to us or which ones we might take an interest in: a fairly terrifying prospect. The television blared and patients in various stages of decompensation paced relentlessly, sat listlessly, or generally appeared to be acting “crazy.

A Stubborn Resistance Resolved in Conjoint Modern Analysis and Hypnotherapy

Richard Friedman PHD

Richard Friedman

1123 Park Ave
New York, NY 10128
Phone: 212 289-3592
Email: drrichardfriedman@gmail.com

Richard Friedman   Graduate of CMPS and a contributor to this journal since 1977, has been a faculty member, supervisor, or training analyst in nine psychotherapy or psychoanalytic programs, including, currently, the China American Psychoanalytic Alliance. He is also a member of the American Society of Clinical Hypnosis.

What psychoanalyst hasn’t had a person who has been in analysis for many years come into the office one day and announce that she had just read an article or had a conversation or seen

222

a movie that had changed her life? The person will have experienced, outside of session, an emotionally significant feeling that the analyst had tried but failed to get at in treatment. This has happened to me many times, and while I am always a little annoyed that I am not getting credit, I am also relieved that a long-standing resistance has at last been resolved. I have talked about the phenomenon with many colleagues who have had similar experiences. In this paper I will discuss how I was instrumental in helping resolve a resistance for someone in treatment with another psychoanalyst, and some implications for this phenomenon of extra-analytic resistance resolution. This article will touch on related topics of split transferences and conjoint treatment.

All psychoanalysts have observed analysands working with extra-analytic transferences—to teachers, coaches, bosses, medical doctors, clergy, even distant celebrities—and perhaps have also noticed that their patients experience things with these extra-analytic figures that they do not experience with their analyst. However, most psychoanalysts, or at least most psychoanalysts who have published writings, don’t like split transferences. They feel it somehow dilutes the treatment (Wallerstein, 2000). Some modern analysts, however, acknowledge both the inevitability of split transference—for example, when an analysand is both in analysis and simultaneously in supervision—and also the potential usefulness of the split (London, 1989; Unger, 1978). With the partial exceptions of working with a psychoanalyst or student-psychoanalyst patient who is in supervision, or a patient who is sent to another analyst for couples therapy or group therapy, however, most of these extra-psychoanalytic transferences are serendipitous. That is true of the case I’m presenting here. I know from subsequent conversations that the referring psychoanalyst did not intend to create a split transference. Her only conscious intention was to offer me as a resource to help her patient with a highly specific problem that she hoped I could resolve very quickly. What we both learned from our joint work with this person is it that sometimes split transference can be a useful experience and perhaps could be something that an analyst might intentionally try to create.
